text: The nested loop `for r... for (c = r+1)...` performs n(n-1)/2 iterations, exactly half of `c = 0`. Why is it still O(n²)?
choices: Because the inner loop's bound depends on r, which makes the analysis non-constant.
Because the two loops are nested, and nesting always yields the square regardless of bounds.
Big-O discards constant factors, so halving the work is a real improvement the notation cannot express.
It is not — starting from r+1 makes it O(n log n), since the work per row shrinks.
explanation: The definition excludes constant factors via c and small inputs via n₀, deliberately. n²/2 - n/2 is O(n²): the 1/2 goes and the -n/2 goes. Verified, each doubling multiplied the pair count by exactly 4.00, which is the quadratic signature and is unaffected by the halving. Half the running time is still half the running time; the notation is measuring something else.
